title: Who are my mother and brothers? (Mark 3:31–35)
hookLine: whoever does God's will is family

lines: A HOUSE PACKED TO THE WALLS.
cards: Picture the house: packed wall to wall, people sitting on the floor around Jesus, listening. Outside, at the door, his mother and his brothers, come to bring him home.

They can't get in, so they send a message through the crowd, hand to hand, the way you'd pass a note in class. Your mother and your brothers are outside, asking for you. Every head turns to see what he'll do.
Most of us know exactly what we'd do. We'd get up. Jesus answers with a question.

teach.b: He asks: who is my mother, or my brethren? Then, in the King James Bible, "he looked round about on them which sat about him, and said, Behold my mother and my brethren!"
He looks at the circle on the floor: fishermen, a tax collector, neighbors, strangers.

teach.h: WHOSOEVER SHALL DO THE WILL OF GOD.
teach.b: "For whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and mother." Notice the last line. In the King James, the message at the door named his mother and his brothers.
His answer adds a sister. The circle keeps getting wider. It can sound cold, turning away his own mother.
Christians don't usually read it that way. Most hear the family made bigger, not smaller: the door open to anyone.
And they point out that Mary appears again later, near the cross in John's gospel and praying with the disciples in Acts, so she's in the circle too.

The brothers raise a question churches answer differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians understand them as close relatives, cousins, or Joseph's sons from an earlier marriage, holding that Mary remained a virgin.
Many Protestants understand them as younger children of Mary and Joseph. Both read the same Greek word, brother.

teach.h: THE END OF MARK ONE TO THREE.
teach.b: And that closes the first part of Mark, three breathless chapters: a voice in the wilderness, the sky torn open, fishermen leaving nets, a man with leprosy, a roof dug through, Levi's table, a withered hand, twelve names, a house divided.
It ends here, with a new kind of family sitting on the floor. Next: seeds, storms and loaves.

how: Many Christians call one another brother and sister, and churches often describe themselves as a family of faith, drawing on Jesus's words that whoever does the will of God is his brother, sister and mother.

games.why: he looks around at those sitting with him: behold my mother and my brethren. whoever does the will of God is family.

practice: Picture the people who've been family to you without sharing your blood: the neighbor who took you in, the friend who shows up every birthday, the coach, the roommate, the church aunt, the colleague who covered for you.
Choose one face and remember one specific thing they did. If you pray, thank God for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Brethren, who Jesus named as he looked around the circle on the floor: whoever does God's will, now called brother, sister and mother too.

orig.note: Greek: brother, literally from the same womb. It also stretched to kin and to fellow believers.

carryVoice: Your line: family is wider. Three chapters of Mark end on a crowded floor. That's day one hundred seventy.
